# The generated code

`urn-forge compile` writes `domain.generated.ts` in the output folder (`src/generated` by default). With `postgres` in the config, `compile` also writes `schema.generated.sql` and `domain.store.generated.ts`. Refer to [The Postgres schema](./postgres-schema).

## The header

```
// Generated by urn-forge from domain.manifest.yaml. Do not edit: change the manifest, then run urn-forge compile.
// fingerprint sha256:…
/* eslint-disable */
import * as v from 'valibot';
```

The path is the manifest, relative to the config file. The fingerprint is the SHA-256 of the body of the file. The same manifest always gives the same file.

## The import

The file imports one package, `valibot`, as `v`. `valibot` is a dependency of `urn-forge`, so the install of urn-forge also installs the version of Valibot that urn-forge is tested with. The file does not import `urn-forge`. The other helpers that it needs, such as `$eq` and `$timestamp`, are copied into it.

## Names

The TypeScript name of a definition is its name in PascalCase: `party_size` gives `PartySize`. If the name is one of the names that the file declares itself (`Failure`, `RuleError`, `DomainCore`, `Operations`, `Definitions`, `OperationName`, `DefinitionName`, `OperationResult` or `CheckResult`), `Value` is added, for example `OperationsValue`.

The name of the schema of a definition is its name in PascalCase and `Schema`: `party_size` gives `PartySizeSchema`. `Value` is not added to the name of a schema.

## Exports

| Export | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| A type for each definition | `type PartySize = number`, `type State = "confirmed" \| …`, `interface Booking { … }`, `type Tables = readonly TableNumber[]`, `type StoredBooking = Booking` |
| A schema for each definition, `<Name>Schema` | A Valibot schema of the definition, with its rules. Refer to [Schemas](#schemas) |
| `Failure` | A rule that a value breaks. Refer to [Failure](#failure) |
| `Definitions` | Each definition: its base type, the items of a list, the properties of an object, and the names of its rules. The Gherkin steps read it |
| `DefinitionName` | The name of a definition |
| `DefinitionTypes` | The TypeScript type of each definition, by name |
| `CheckResult<T>` | `{ ok: true, value }` or `{ ok: false, failures }` |
| `check(definition, value)` | Checks a value against a definition |
| `Answer<O, V>` | An answer of the core: `{ output, value }` |
| `answer(output, value)` | Makes an answer |
| `<Operation>Answer` | The answers of one operation, for example `QuoteShippingAnswer` |
| `DomainCore` | The type of the core: a function for each operation |
| `Operations` | Each operation: its input and its outputs. The Gherkin steps read it |
| `OperationName` | The name of an operation |
| `OperationResult<N>` | The result of `runOperation` |
| `runOperation(core, operation, input)` | The harness |

A definition, an operation or a property with `deprecated: true` has `@deprecated` in its comment.

## Schemas

Each definition has a Valibot schema, `<Name>Schema`. A Valibot schema is a [Standard Schema](https://standardschema.dev), so a library that takes a Standard Schema can use it, such as tRPC, Hono or a form library.

| Definition | Schema |
| --- | --- |
| `string` | `v.string()` |
| `integer` | `v.number()` and `v.integer()` in a pipe |
| `number` | `v.number()` and `v.finite()` in a pipe |
| `boolean` | `v.boolean()` |
| `array` | `v.array()` of the schema of `items` |
| `object` | `v.strictObject()` of the schema of each property. A property that is not in `required` is `v.optional()` |
| A definition with another definition as its `type` | The schema of that definition. Its own rules are in a pipe |
| A definition that a cycle reaches again | `v.lazy()` |

Each rule is a `v.check` in the pipe of the schema. The `required` rule of an object is not in the pipe: it is the structure of `v.strictObject()`. The helper `$rule` makes the check:

```ts
/** A rule in the pipe of a schema: a Valibot check whose requirement keeps the definition and the rule's name. */
function $rule(definition: string, rule: string, message: string, test: (value: any) => boolean) {
  return v.check<any, string>(Object.assign((value: unknown) => $holds(() => test(value)), { definition, rule }), message);
}
```

These are schemas of the booking fixture, `tests/fixtures/booking/generated/domain.generated.ts`:

```ts
/** The number of guests */
export const PartySizeSchema = v.pipe(v.pipe(v.number('Must be an integer'), v.integer('Must be an integer')),
  $rule("party_size", "minimum", "Must be at least 1", (value: any) => ((value as any) >= (1 as any))),
  $rule("party_size", "maximum", "Must be at most 12", (value: any) => ((value as any) <= (12 as any))));

/** How to reach the guest */
export const ContactSchema = v.strictObject({ email: EmailSchema, phone: v.optional(PhoneSchema) }, 'Must be an object');

/** The booking as it is stored, before the call */
export const StoredBookingSchema = BookingSchema;
```

The requirement of each `v.check` keeps the definition and the name of the rule. The message of the check is the `message` of the rule, with its arguments filled. Thus a Valibot issue of a rule has the same text as the failure of `check`:

```ts
import * as v from 'valibot';
import { PartySizeSchema } from './generated/domain.generated';

const result = v.safeParse(PartySizeSchema, 13);
```

`result.issues` has one issue. These are its `type`, its `message`, and the `definition` and `rule` of its `requirement`:

```json
[{"type":"check","message":"Must be at most 12","requirement":{"definition":"party_size","rule":"maximum"}}]
```

Through the Standard Schema interface, `PartySizeSchema['~standard'].validate(13)` gives an issue with the message `Must be at most 12`. The vendor is `valibot`.

Valibot runs the pipe of an object only after its properties parse. Thus a rule of an object reads only properties of the correct type.

`check` and `runOperation` use the schemas. They give the failures of [Failure](#failure), not the issues of Valibot.

## DomainCore

```ts
/** The core: a function for each operation, from its input to one of its answers. */
export interface DomainCore {
  /** Calculate the price to send a parcel */
  readonly quote_shipping: (input: Parcel) => QuoteShippingAnswer;
}
```

The core exports a value that `satisfies DomainCore`. Gate 1 of `verify` checks it. Each function is synchronous.

## answer

```ts
export function answer<O extends string, V>(output: O, value: V): Answer<O, V> {
  return { output, value };
}
```

`answer('quote', { price_cents: 600 })` is an answer of the output `quote`. TypeScript checks the name and the value against `<Operation>Answer`.

## runOperation

```ts
export function runOperation<N extends OperationName>(core: DomainCore, operation: N, input: unknown): OperationResult<N>
```

It does these steps:

1. It checks `input` against the input definition. If a rule breaks, it returns `kind: 'InputRejected'`, and the core does not run.
2. It calls `core[operation](input)`.
3. It checks that the answer names an output of the operation, then checks the value against the definition of that output.
4. It checks the rules of that output, then the rules of the operation.
5. If step 3 or step 4 fails, it returns `kind: 'ContractViolation'`. Otherwise, it returns the answer.

If the core throws an exception, `runOperation` does not catch it.

## OperationResult

```ts
export type OperationResult<N extends OperationName = OperationName> =
  | ({ readonly ok: true; readonly operation: N } & ReturnType<DomainCore[N]>)
  | { readonly ok: false; readonly operation: N; readonly kind: 'InputRejected' | 'ContractViolation'; readonly failures: readonly Failure[] };
```

| Result | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `ok: true` | The answer keeps the contract. `output` is the name of the output, and `value` its value. TypeScript narrows `value` by `output` |
| `ok: false`, `kind: 'InputRejected'` | The caller sent an input that breaks the contract |
| `ok: false`, `kind: 'ContractViolation'` | The core answered what the contract does not allow. This is a bug in the core |

For the shipping domain, these are real results:

```json
{"ok":true,"operation":"quote_shipping","output":"quote","value":{"price_cents":800}}
{"ok":true,"operation":"quote_shipping","output":"too_heavy_for_express","value":{"weight_grams":6000}}
```

```json
{
  "ok": false,
  "operation": "quote_shipping",
  "kind": "InputRejected",
  "failures": [
    {
      "definition": "weight_grams",
      "rule": "minimum",
      "path": "weight_grams",
      "message": "Must be at least 1"
    },
    {
      "definition": "zone",
      "rule": "enum",
      "path": "zone",
      "message": "Must be one of domestic, international"
    }
  ]
}
```

## Failure

Each failure has four properties:

| Property | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `definition` | The definition whose rule broke. For a rule of an output or of an operation, the name of the operation |
| `rule` | The name of the rule. For the structure of a value: `type` (a wrong type), `properties` (a key that is not a property), `required` (an absent required property) or `output` (an answer that is not an output of the operation) |
| `path` | The place of the value, such as `weight_grams`, `contact.email` or `dishes[0].amount`. In a check of the value of an answer, the path starts with `output`, such as `output.price_cents`. It is `''` for the whole value, and for a rule of an output or an operation |
| `message` | The `message` of the rule, with its arguments filled |

An application can show its own text for a rule, by the name in `rule`.

The generated file declares and exports the type `Failure`: `import type { Failure } from './generated/domain.generated'`. It does not come from Valibot or from `urn-forge`. `check` and `runOperation` make a failure from each issue of Valibot:

- an issue of a `v.check` gives the definition and the rule of its requirement;
- a value of the wrong type gives `type`;
- a key that is not a property gives `properties`;
- absent required properties give one `required` failure of the object.

## check

```ts
export function check<D extends DefinitionName>(definition: D, value: unknown): CheckResult<DefinitionTypes[D]>
```

`check` checks a value against one definition, without an operation. The shell can use it to check a value before it stores it. The Gherkin step `When I check a "<definition>" with:` uses it.

```json
{
  "ok": false,
  "failures": [
    {
      "definition": "quote",
      "rule": "properties",
      "path": "currency",
      "message": "Must be one of the properties of quote: price_cents"
    }
  ]
}
```

This is the result of `check('quote', { price_cents: 600, currency: 'EUR' })`.
